title: Explain the full flow of a microservices application (client → API Gateway → service discovery → service → DB → inter-service calls → response → logging/tracing).
shortTitle: Explain the full flow of a microservices application end to end

s1_definition.profdef: The full flow of a microservices request is the ordered path a single call takes from a client through the system and back: the client sends an HTTPS request to an API Gateway, which authenticates it, applies rate limiting, and routes it to the right service, resolving that service's live network address through service discovery; the chosen service runs its business logic against its own database, and where it needs data owned by another service it makes an inter-service call, again resolved through discovery and protected by timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker; the service builds a response that flows back through the gateway to the client, and throughout the path every hop emits structured logs and carries a correlation and trace identifier so the whole journey can be reconstructed in a distributed tracing tool.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India to make a transfer. The security guard at the main door, the API Gateway, checks his ID, makes sure he is not flooding the branch with requests, and points him to the correct counter. A branch directory, service discovery, tells the guard which transfer counters are currently open and staffed. At the transfer counter, the officer does the work using the transfer department's own files, the service database. To confirm Rajesh's identity details the officer phones the accounts department, an inter-service call, and if that department is not answering the officer waits only a few seconds, tries once more, and then stops calling for a while rather than freezing the queue, which is the circuit breaker. The officer hands Rajesh a receipt, the response, and every step is written in the branch logbook with the same reference number so an auditor can follow Rajesh's entire visit end to end.
s1_definition.oneliner: A request flows client to gateway to discovery to service to database, makes resilient inter-service calls when it needs another service's data, returns the response back through the gateway, and the whole journey is stitched together by a correlation identifier in structured logs and distributed traces.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The full flow of a microservices request is the ordered path a single call takes from a client through the system and back: the client sends an HTTPS request to an API Gateway, which authenticates it, applies rate limiting, and routes it to the right service, resolving that service's live network address through service discovery; the chosen service runs its business logic against its own database, and where it needs data owned by another service it makes an inter-service call, again resolved through discovery and protected by timeouts, retries, and a circuit breaker; the service builds a response that flows back through the gateway to the client, and throughout the path every hop emits structured logs and carries a correlation and trace identifier so the whole journey can be reconstructed in a distributed tracing tool.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine Rajesh walks into National Bank of India to make a transfer. The security guard at the main door, the API Gateway, checks his ID, makes sure he is not flooding the branch with requests, and points him to the correct counter. A branch directory, service discovery, tells the guard which transfer counters are currently open and staffed. At the transfer counter, the officer does the work using the transfer department's own files, the service database. To confirm Rajesh's identity details the officer phones the accounts department, an inter-service call, and if that department is not answering the officer waits only a few seconds, tries once more, and then stops calling for a while rather than freezing the queue, which is the circuit breaker. The officer hands Rajesh a receipt, the response, and every step is written in the branch logbook with the same reference number so an auditor can follow Rajesh's entire visit end to end.

**One line to remember:** A request flows client to gateway to discovery to service to database, makes resilient inter-service calls when it needs another service's data, returns the response back through the gateway, and the whole journey is stitched together by a correlation identifier in structured logs and distributed traces.

sections.s2_technical:
Begin at the edge with the client and the API Gateway. The client, a mobile app or web front end, sends an HTTPS request to one public address, the gateway, rather than to individual services. The gateway is the single front door and it does the cross-cutting work so each service does not have to: it terminates TLS, authenticates the caller by validating the JWT or OAuth2 token, applies rate limiting and quota to protect the system from floods, and routes the request to the correct backend based on the path, for example sending `/api/v1/transfers` to the transfer service. Centralising these concerns at the gateway keeps the individual services focused on business logic and gives one place to enforce security.

Next is service discovery, which answers "where is the transfer service right now?" In a dynamic environment, service instances come and go as they scale and get rescheduled, so their addresses are not fixed. A registry such as Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes' built-in DNS and Services holds the current set of healthy instances for each service name. The gateway, and later any service making an inter-service call, asks discovery for the current instances and picks one, usually with a client-side load balancer that spreads calls across them. This is why you never hardcode an instance IP: you call by logical name and discovery resolves it to a live, healthy address.

Then the request reaches the chosen service instance, where the actual business logic runs. The service receives the request in its controller, validates the input, and calls its service layer, which executes the domain logic, for example checking balance and moving money. The service owns its own database, and only this service reads and writes that database directly, which is the database-per-service rule that keeps services decoupled. It uses a connection pool and, for a write like a transfer, a local transaction so the debit and credit either both happen or neither does.

Inter-service calls happen when a service needs data or an action that belongs to another service, because no service reaches into another's database. There are two styles. Synchronous calls use REST or gRPC: the transfer service calls the accounts service's API and waits for the answer, which is simple but couples their availability, so you wrap such calls in a timeout so a slow dependency cannot hang the caller, a small number of retries for transient failures ideally made idempotent, a circuit breaker that stops calling a failing dependency and fails fast or serves a fallback, and a bulkhead that isolates the thread pool so one slow dependency cannot exhaust all the caller's threads. Asynchronous calls use messaging like Kafka: the service publishes an event such as "transfer completed" and moves on, and other services consume it on their own schedule, which decouples availability and smooths load at the cost of eventual consistency. A good system uses synchronous calls where it needs an immediate answer and events where it can tolerate eventual processing.

Then the response flows back. The service builds a response object, the controller serializes it, and it travels back through the gateway to the client, often with the gateway adding or stripping headers. If the service published events, downstream work like notifications and audit continues asynchronously after the client already has its answer, so the user is not kept waiting for non-essential steps.

Cutting across every one of these hops are logging and tracing, which is what makes a distributed system debuggable. When the request enters the gateway, it is tagged with a correlation identifier, and that identifier is propagated on every downstream call through headers, so all log lines for one user request share the same identifier and can be gathered from every service into a central store like the ELK stack. Distributed tracing goes further: each hop creates a span with a start and end time, parent and child spans are linked by trace context propagated in headers, for example the W3C traceparent header, and a tool like Jaeger or Zipkin shows the whole request as a waterfall across services, so you can see exactly which call was slow or failed. Metrics from each service, scraped by Prometheus and shown in Grafana, add the aggregate view of latency, error rate, and throughput.

Senior nuances worth stating: keep services stateless so any instance behind discovery can serve any request; propagate the trace and correlation context religiously, because a single missed hop creates a blind spot; prefer events for anything that can be eventual to reduce coupling and improve resilience; design every synchronous dependency assuming it will one day be slow or down, which is why timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads are not optional; and make retried operations idempotent so a retry after a timeout does not double-charge a customer. The combination of discovery, resilient inter-service calls, and end-to-end tracing is what separates a robust microservices system from a fragile distributed monolith.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A customer of National Bank of India opens the mobile app and requests a transfer, but the app should not need to know the address of every internal service, and the bank must authenticate and rate-limit the request in one place. This is exactly what the API Gateway solves, acting as the single secured front door that routes to the right service.

Problem 2 — The transfer service runs as several instances that scale up and down, so its address changes, and callers must always reach a live, healthy instance. This is exactly what service discovery solves, resolving a logical service name to a current healthy instance.

Problem 3 — To complete a transfer the transfer service needs to confirm the destination account exists, which is owned by the accounts service, and the accounts service might be slow or down. This is exactly what resilient inter-service calls solve, using a timeout, a retry, and a circuit breaker so a sick dependency does not freeze transfers.

Problem 4 — When a transfer fails somewhere in this chain, an engineer must find out which hop failed across several services. This is exactly what correlation identifiers and distributed tracing solve, stitching one request's journey across all services.

Our mini-project simulates the full flow in one runnable demo: a gateway step that authenticates and routes, a discovery step that resolves the transfer service, the transfer service doing the debit and credit against its database, a resilient inter-service call to the accounts service guarded by timeout and circuit breaker, and a correlation identifier carried through every log line.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash

javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/flow/FullFlowDemo.java
java -cp target/classes com.bank.flow.FullFlowDemo

# In a real system, the same flow would be exercised with:
curl -X POST https://api.bank.in/api/v1/transfers \

  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"from":"SAV2001","to":"CUR3001","amount":50000}'
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a transfer request of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh (SAV2001) to Priya (CUR3001), with a valid JWT, arriving at the public gateway address.

Step 1: The request hits the API Gateway. The gateway generates a correlation and trace identifier, say trace `a1b2c3d4`, validates the JWT, and confirms the caller is under the rate limit. The data at this point is the raw HTTP request plus the new trace identifier attached to it.

Step 2: The gateway asks service discovery for a live instance of the transfer service. The registry returns one of two healthy instances by round-robin, say 10.0.0.11:8080. The data is the logical name in, a concrete healthy address out.

Step 3: The gateway routes the request to that transfer-service instance, carrying the trace identifier in a header. The transfer service receives from SAV2001, to CUR3001, amount fifty thousand.

Step 4: The transfer service must confirm the destination account is valid, which is owned by the accounts service, so it makes a synchronous inter-service call through the AccountsClient. The call is guarded by a timeout and a circuit breaker. The accounts service answers that CUR3001 exists. If it had been down five times, the breaker would open and the client would fail fast with a cached fallback instead of hanging.

Step 5: With the destination confirmed, the transfer service runs its business logic against its own database. It checks Rajesh's balance of one million, debits fifty thousand to leave nine hundred fifty thousand, and credits Priya from two hundred fifty thousand to three hundred thousand, inside a local transaction.

Step 6: The transfer service returns success to the gateway, which returns 201 Created to the client. The client now has its answer. Any non-essential follow-up, such as publishing a transfer.completed event for notification and audit, happens asynchronously after this point.

Step 7: Throughout steps 1 to 6 every component logged a line tagged with trace `a1b2c3d4`, and each hop created a span. The ELK stack gathers all the log lines by that trace, and Jaeger shows the request as a waterfall: gateway span, discovery lookup, transfer-service span, and the nested accounts-service call, with timings, so any slow or failed hop is immediately visible.

Final output:

```
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] GATEWAY received POST /api/v1/transfers
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] GATEWAY auth OK, rate-limit OK
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] DISCOVERY transfer-service → 10.0.0.11:8080
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] ACCOUNTS exists(CUR3001)=true
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] TRANSFER done SAV2001→CUR3001 Rs.50000
2026-10-24 15:10:30 INFO    [a1b2c3d4] GATEWAY returning 201 Created to client
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Client (mobile app): POST /api/v1/transfers {from,to,amount} + JWT
    │ HTTPS
    ▼
  API Gateway  [trace a1b2c3d4 created]
    │ validate JWT ✓   rate-limit ✓   route /api/v1/transfers
    ▼
  Service Discovery (registry)
    │ resolve "transfer-service" → 10.0.0.11:8080  (round-robin over 2 instances)
    ▼
  Transfer Service (instance 10.0.0.11)
    │ needs destination validity (owned by Accounts) 
    │   ├── inter-service call ──→ Accounts Service  [timeout 2s + circuit breaker]
    │   │                            exists(CUR3001)=true
    │   ▼
    │ own DB: Rajesh 1,000,000 → 950,000 ; Priya 250,000 → 300,000  (local txn)
    ▼
  Response 201 Created ──→ Gateway ──→ Client
    │
    └── async: publish "transfer.completed" → Kafka → Audit + Notification

  Cross-cutting: every hop logs [a1b2c3d4] → ELK ; each hop = span → Jaeger waterfall
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The full flow of a microservices application is the path one request takes from the client and back, and I describe it hop by hop. The client sends an HTTPS request to the API Gateway, which is the single secured front door; it terminates TLS, validates the token, applies rate limiting, and routes the request to the right service, so the services themselves stay focused on business logic. To route, the gateway uses service discovery, a registry such as Eureka, Consul, or Kubernetes Services, which resolves a logical service name to a currently healthy instance and lets a client-side load balancer spread the calls, which is why we never hardcode instance addresses.

The request then reaches the chosen service instance, which runs its business logic against its own database following the database-per-service rule, so no other service touches that data directly. Where it needs data owned by another service it makes an inter-service call, and here resilience is the whole game. Synchronous calls over REST or gRPC give an immediate answer but couple availability, so I wrap them in a timeout, a small number of idempotent retries, a circuit breaker that fails fast when a dependency is sick, and a bulkhead that isolates threads. Asynchronous calls over Kafka publish an event and move on, which decouples the services and smooths load at the cost of eventual consistency, so I use synchronous calls when I need an answer now and events for anything that can be eventual, like notifications and audit.

The response then flows back through the gateway to the client, and any non-essential follow-up continues asynchronously after the client already has its answer. Cutting across every hop are logging and tracing, which are what make a distributed system debuggable: the gateway tags the request with a correlation and trace identifier, every service propagates it in headers, the ELK stack gathers all log lines for one request by that identifier, and a tracing tool like Jaeger shows the request as a waterfall of spans across services so I can see exactly which call was slow or failed, while Prometheus and Grafana give the aggregate latency, error rate, and throughput.

On my project at National Bank of India this is exactly how a transfer flowed: the gateway authenticated and routed, discovery resolved one of several transfer-service instances, the transfer service did the debit and credit on its own database, and it made a guarded call to the accounts service to validate the destination, where a circuit breaker once saved us by failing fast with a cached fallback when accounts was overloaded during a deployment, so transfers kept working instead of hanging. The single most valuable thing we built was disciplined correlation-identifier and trace propagation, because the first time a transfer failed intermittently we found the slow hop in Jaeger in minutes instead of guessing across five services.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that a request flows client to gateway to discovery to the owning service to its database, makes resilient inter-service calls guarded by timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, and bulkheads when it needs another service's data or uses events when it can be eventual, returns the response through the gateway, and is stitched together end to end by a correlation identifier in structured logs and distributed traces, because without that observability a microservices system is impossible to debug.
